title: Amendment 3 passed. What it means for your Florida condo's tax bill, and the dates to watch
seoTitle: Florida Amendment 3 Passed: What Condo Owners Should Know
description: Amendment 3 passed Nov. 3. What changes for homestead condos, second homes and rentals, when it hits tax bills, and the dates Florida condo owners need.
dek: Voters approved the property tax amendment on Tuesday. For condo owners, the change depends on one question: is the unit your homestead? Here is what changes, what stays the same, and when you will see it on a bill.
facebook: Amendment 3 passed. So what happens to your condo's tax bill? It depends on whether the unit is your homestead, and you won't see it on a bill until November 2027. Here's what changes, what doesn't, and the dates to watch.
keywords: does Amendment 3 lower my condo property taxes
Amendment 3 new Florida residents fifth year

body.text: On Tuesday, November 3, Florida voters approved Amendment 3, the property tax amendment. It passed with about 62% of the vote when the race was called, according to CBS12. A constitutional amendment needs at least 60%. The results are unofficial until the state certifies them.

Two weeks ago The Breezeway explained what the amendment would do if it passed. Now it has. This article covers what that means for condo owners, what does not change, and the dates that matter. It is a guide to what the amendment says, not tax advice. For your own unit, your county property appraiser is the office to ask.

body.title: Terms to know
body.text: Homestead: your permanent Florida home, with a homestead exemption on file with the county property appraiser. Exemption: an amount taken off the value your taxes are figured on. Assessed value: the value the property appraiser uses for taxes, which can be lower than market value. Non-school taxes: everything on your tax bill except the school board's share, such as county, city and special district taxes. Non-homestead: any other property, like a second home, a winter condo or a rental unit.
If your condo is your homestead
The amendment raises the homestead exemption for non-school taxes. The Sarasota County Property Appraiser puts today's amount at $51,411 for 2026. Under the official ballot text:

items: Starting January 1, 2027, the exemption from non-school taxes is up to $150,000 of assessed value.
Starting January 1, 2028, it is up to $250,000. After that it is adjusted each year for inflation.
School taxes do not get the bigger exemption. The school-tax exemption stays at up to $25,000, so most homestead owners will still get a school tax bill.

Save Our Homes stays. That is the cap that limits how fast a homestead's assessed value can rise each year. The Sarasota County Property Appraiser says the amendment does not require homesteads to be reassessed to market value. Portability and existing exemptions for veterans and widows or widowers also remain.

body.text: The amendment does not erase the bill. It lowers the value that county, city and special district taxes are figured on. How much you save depends on your unit's assessed value and on the tax rates your local governments set each year.

There is a date written into the amendment. People who had a permanent residence in Florida on December 31, 2026 can get the larger amounts. People who had not get the smaller, existing exemption of up to $50,000 for non-school taxes when they first qualify. Starting with the fifth year of their exemption, they can get the larger amount.

This matters in condo buildings, where many owners split the year between Florida and somewhere else. Whether you count as a permanent Florida resident is decided under Florida law by your county property appraiser, not by your association. If you are not sure where you stand, call the property appraiser's office before the end of the year and ask.
If your condo is a second home or a rental

Units that are not homesteads do not get the bigger exemption. What changes for them is the yearly cap. Starting January 1, 2027, the assessed value of a non-homestead property can rise at most 5% a year for non-school taxes, down from 10%.

The Sarasota County Property Appraiser gives an example. A unit with a prior-year assessed value of $300,000 could rise to as much as $330,000 under the old cap. Under the new cap, the most is $315,000. Two things to keep in mind. The cap limits how fast assessed value grows; it does not cut tax rates. And school taxes are not covered by this cap.

items: Your association fees. Monthly or quarterly condo assessments come from the association's budget. Nothing in the amendment deals with association budgets, reserves, SIRS funding or special assessments.
School taxes. The school board's share of your bill keeps the current rules.

Who sets tax rates. Counties, cities, school boards and special districts still set their own rates each year. The amendment also lists what counties and cities may spend property tax money on, such as public safety, schools, roads and infrastructure.

body.text: On the money side for local governments, a legislative analysis estimated nearly $5 billion less in local revenue in the 2027-28 budget year, CBS News Miami reported. How each county and city responds is up to their own budgets.

items: December 31, 2026: the residency date in the amendment.
January 1, 2027: the amendment takes effect, for the 2027 tax roll.

March 1: the usual deadline to file a homestead application for that year with your county property appraiser. To qualify, you generally must own the property and make it your permanent residence on January 1.
November 2027: the first tax bills that show the changes, according to the Sarasota and Seminole county property appraisers.
January 1, 2028: the non-school homestead exemption rises to up to $250,000.
Look up your unit on your county property appraiser's website. It shows whether a homestead exemption is on file.
If your condo is your permanent home and no homestead is on file, ask the property appraiser how to apply before March 1.
If you moved to Florida recently or split your year, ask the property appraiser how the December 31, 2026 date applies to you.
If you own more than one unit, look at each one on its own. A homestead and a rental are treated differently.
Don't budget on a guess. Your actual savings depend on 2027 values and local tax rates. Watch for your 2027 notice of proposed taxes and the November 2027 bill.
Expect questions at the next meeting. A short, neutral answer helps: the amendment is about property taxes, not association fees, and the 2027 budget process is unchanged.
Point owners to the county property appraiser for questions about their own unit.
If the board is unsure whether anything in the amendment touches the association's own property or budget, ask the association attorney or accountant.

faq.a: Yes. It passed on November 3, 2026 with about 62% of the vote when the race was called, above the 60% needed. Results are unofficial until the state certifies them.
January 1, 2027. County property appraisers say the first tax bills that reflect it arrive in November 2027.

faq.q: Does Amendment 3 lower my condo HOA fees?
faq.a: No. It deals with property taxes. Condo association fees come from the association's budget, which the amendment does not change.

faq.q: Does Amendment 3 help my second-home condo?
faq.a: Non-homestead units do not get the larger exemption. Starting January 1, 2027, their assessed value for non-school taxes can rise at most 5% a year instead of 10%. That slows growth in assessed value; it does not cut tax rates.

faq.q: I'm moving to Florida in 2027. Do I get the $150,000 exemption?
faq.a: Under the amendment, people who did not have a permanent residence in Florida on December 31, 2026 get the existing exemption of up to $50,000 for non-school taxes, and can get the larger amount starting in the fifth year of their exemption. Your county property appraiser can tell you how it applies to you.
